subject: Computer Engineering Mathematics II
learning_objective: Derive and interpret the sampled spectrum of a signal composed of components with different bandwidths.
question_text:
Consider the continuous-time signal
\[x(t)=\operatorname{sinc}\left(\frac{\pi t}{\tau}\right)+\frac12\operatorname{sinc}\left(\frac{2\pi t}{\tau}\right),\quad \tau>0.\]
It is uniformly sampled by \[p(t)=\sum_{m=-\infty}^{\infty}\delta\left(t-\frac{m\tau}{5}\right),\qquad g(t)=x(t)p(t).\]
Use \(X(j\omega)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(t)e^{-j\omega t}\,dt\) and \(\operatorname{sinc}(u)=\sin(u)/u\) (with sinc(0)=1).
1. (1 point) Derive \(X(j\omega)\) and identify its frequency support.
2. (1 point) Derive \(P(j\omega)\) and identify frequency spacing between impulses.
3. (1 point) Express \(g(t)\) as a weighted impulse train. Determine impulse weights at \(t=0\) and \(t=\pm\tau\).
4. (1 point) Derive \(G(j\omega)\) in terms of shifted copies of \(X(j\omega)\).
5. (1 point) Sketch the magnitude spectra of \(X\) and \(G\), labeling heights, boundaries and replica centers. Explain whether spectral overlapping occurs.
solution:
Step 1 — Apply the sinc transform pair and time scaling:
\[\mathcal F\{\operatorname{sinc}(\pi t/\tau)\}=\tau\operatorname{rect}(\omega\tau/(2\pi)),\]
\[\mathcal F\{\tfrac12\operatorname{sinc}(2\pi t/\tau)\}=\tfrac\tau4\operatorname{rect}(\omega\tau/(4\pi)).\]
Therefore \[X(j\omega)=\tau\operatorname{rect}(\omega\tau/(2\pi))+\tfrac\tau4\operatorname{rect}(\omega\tau/(4\pi)).\]
Its levels are \(5\tau/4\) for \(|\omega|<\pi/\tau\), \(\tau/4\) for \(\pi/\tau<|\omega|<2\pi/\tau\), and 0 outside \(|\omega|>2\pi/\tau\).
Step 2 — Sampling period \(T_s=\tau/5\), angular spacing \(\omega_s=10\pi/\tau\):
\[P(j\omega)=\frac{10\pi}{\tau}\sum_k\delta(\omega-10\pi k/\tau).\]
Step 3 — Sample weights:
\[g(t)=\sum_m w_m\delta(t-m\tau/5),\quad w_m=\operatorname{sinc}(\pi m/5)+\tfrac12\operatorname{sinc}(2\pi m/5).\]
At \(m=0\), \(w_0=3/2\). At \(m=\pm5\), both sinc terms vanish, so \(w_{\pm5}=0\).
Step 4 — Multiplication in time corresponds to frequency convolution:
\[G(j\omega)=\frac1{T_s}\sum_kX(j(\omega-\omega_s k))=\frac5\tau\sum_k X(j(\omega-10\pi k/\tau)).\]
Let \(\Omega_k=\omega-10\pi k/\tau\). Then
\[G(j\omega)=\sum_k\left[5\operatorname{rect}(\Omega_k\tau/(2\pi))+\tfrac54\operatorname{rect}(\Omega_k\tau/(4\pi))\right].\]
Step 5 — For each center \(\omega_k=10\pi k/\tau\), height is \(25/4\) within \(|\omega-\omega_k|<\pi/\tau\), \(5/4\) in the outer band up to \(2\pi/\tau\), and 0 beyond. Sketch each replica with these two levels. Since \(\omega_s=10\pi/\tau>4\pi/\tau\), replicas do not overlap (no aliasing).
final_answer: \(w_0=3/2,\;w_{\pm5}=0\). \(G(j\omega)=\frac5\tau\sum_kX(j(\omega-10\pi k/\tau))\), with two-level nonoverlapping replicas centered at \(10\pi k/\tau\).

generation_rationale: Different from REF_001: a sum of sinc signals with two distinct bandwidths produces a two-level rather than a single rectangular spectrum.

subject: Computer Engineering Mathematics II
learning_objective: Recover a time-domain signal from its frequency-domain representation and predict its sampled spectrum.
question_text:
A continuous-time signal has frequency representation
\[X(j\omega)=\tau\operatorname{rect}\left(\frac{\omega\tau}{2\pi}\right)\left[1+\cos\left(\frac{\omega\tau}{2}\right)\right],\quad\tau>0.\]
Sample using an impulse train of period \(T_s=\tau/4\).
1. (1 point) Find \(x(t)\).
2. (1 point) Express \(g(t)\) as an impulse train and determine weights for \(m=0,\pm2\).
3. (1 point) Derive \(P(j\omega)\) and replica spacing.
4. (1 point) Derive \(G(j\omega)\).
5. (1 point) Sketch central and nearest two replicas, label heights/support and determine aliasing.
solution:
Step 1 — Write \(X=X_0+(e^{j\omega\tau/2}/2)X_0+(e^{-j\omega\tau/2}/2)X_0\), where \(X_0=\tau\operatorname{rect}(\omega\tau/(2\pi))\). Inverse CTFT with time shifting yields
\[x(t)=\operatorname{sinc}(\pi t/\tau)+\tfrac12\operatorname{sinc}(\pi(t+\tau/2)/\tau)+\tfrac12\operatorname{sinc}(\pi(t-\tau/2)/\tau).\]
Step 2 — At \(t_m=m\tau/4\), sample weights are
\[w_m=\operatorname{sinc}(\pi m/4)+\tfrac12\operatorname{sinc}(\pi(m+2)/4)+\tfrac12\operatorname{sinc}(\pi(m-2)/4).\]
Thus \(g(t)=\sum_mw_m\delta(t-m\tau/4)\). Using sinc(0)=1 and sinc(π/2)=2/π: \(w_0=1+2/\pi\), \(w_{\pm2}=1/2+2/\pi\).
Step 3 — \(\omega_s=2\pi/T_s=8\pi/\tau\), so
\[P(j\omega)=\frac{8\pi}{\tau}\sum_k\delta(\omega-8\pi k/\tau).\]
Step 4 — Define \(\Omega_k=\omega-8\pi k/\tau\). Spectral sampling produces
\[G(j\omega)=4\sum_k\operatorname{rect}(\Omega_k\tau/(2\pi))[1+\cos(\Omega_k\tau/2)].\]
Step 5 — Each copy is centered at \(8\pi k/\tau\), supported within \(|\omega-8\pi k/\tau|<\pi/\tau\). At the center the height is 8; approaching the support boundary from within it is 4. Draw curved peaks over each rectangular support (with a jump to zero at the edge). Copies do not overlap because spacing \(8\pi/\tau\) exceeds support width \(2\pi/\tau\).
final_answer: \(x(t)=\operatorname{sinc}(\pi t/\tau)+\tfrac12\operatorname{sinc}(\pi(t+\tau/2)/\tau)+\tfrac12\operatorname{sinc}(\pi(t-\tau/2)/\tau)\); sampled replicas centered at \(8\pi k/\tau\), peak 8, no aliasing.

generation_rationale: Unlike REF_001, start with frequency-domain data and reconstruct the time signal using inverse CTFT and shifts before sampling.

subject: Computer Engineering Mathematics II
learning_objective: Derive the spectrum of a squared-sinc signal and compare the effects of two sampling intervals.
question_text:
Consider \[x(t)=\operatorname{sinc}^2(\pi t/\tau),\quad\tau>0.\]
System A samples at \(T_A=\tau/3\); System B samples at \(T_B=\tau/4\). In both cases \(p_i(t)=\sum_m\delta(t-mT_i)\), \(g_i(t)=x(t)p_i(t)\). You may use the sinc transform pair and multiplication-convolution theorem.
1. (1 point) Derive \(X(j\omega)\) in terms of \(\Lambda(u)=\max(1-|u|,0)\).
2. (1 point) Express \(g_A,g_B\) as weighted impulse trains and find first positive zero-weight indices.
3. (1 point) Derive \(G_A,G_B\).
4. (1 point) Find replica centers, peak heights and bandwidths of both systems.
5. (1 point) Sketch both spectra, compare replica separation and identify aliasing.
solution:
Step 1 — Let \(s(t)=\operatorname{sinc}(\pi t/\tau)\), with \(S(j\omega)=\tau\operatorname{rect}(\omega\tau/(2\pi))\). Since \(x=s^2\), \(X=(S*S)/(2\pi)\). Convolution of two identical rectangles gives
\[X(j\omega)=\tau\Lambda(\omega\tau/(2\pi)),\]
peak \(\tau\), support \(|\omega|\le2\pi/\tau\), full width \(4\pi/\tau\).
Step 2 —
\[g_A(t)=\sum_m\operatorname{sinc}^2(\pi m/3)\delta(t-m\tau/3),\]
\[g_B(t)=\sum_m\operatorname{sinc}^2(\pi m/4)\delta(t-m\tau/4).\]
The first positive zero-weight indices are \(m=3\) and \(m=4\), respectively; at \(m=0\) both weights equal 1.
Step 3 — With \(\omega_{s,A}=6\pi/\tau\) and \(\omega_{s,B}=8\pi/\tau\),
\[G_A(j\omega)=3\sum_k\Lambda((\omega-6\pi k/\tau)\tau/(2\pi)),\]
\[G_B(j\omega)=4\sum_k\Lambda((\omega-8\pi k/\tau)\tau/(2\pi)).\]
Step 4 — A replicas centered at \(6\pi k/\tau\), peak 3, width \(4\pi/\tau\), gaps \(2\pi/\tau\). B replicas centered at \(8\pi k/\tau\), peak 4, width \(4\pi/\tau\), gaps \(4\pi/\tau\).
Step 5 — Sketch triangular replicas with linear slopes extending \(2\pi/\tau\) each side. In both systems \(\omega_s>4\pi/\tau\), so no overlap/aliasing. System B has larger gaps.
final_answer: \(X(j\omega)=\tau\Lambda(\omega\tau/(2\pi))\). Both systems yield nonoverlapping triangular replicas. A: spacing \(6\pi/\tau\), peak 3; B: spacing \(8\pi/\tau\), peak 4. B has greater separation.

generation_rationale: Changes sinc to squared sinc (triangular spectrum) and asks for a comparison of two sampling configurations, not the single rectangular spectrum in REF_001.

subject: Computer Engineering Mathematics II
learning_objective: Infer the original signal and sampling parameters from a known nonoverlapping sampled spectrum.
question_text:
An unknown real continuous-time signal \(x(t)\) is sampled by \(p(t)=\sum_m\delta(t-mT_s)\), giving \(g=xp\). The original signal is bandlimited to \(|\omega|<5\pi/\tau\), \(\tau>0\). The measured \(G(j\omega)\) consists of rectangular bands of height 5, repeated every \(20\pi/\tau\). In the central spectral group, the nonzero intervals are \((-4\pi/\tau,-2\pi/\tau)\) and \((2\pi/\tau,4\pi/\tau)\). Every other group is an identical copy shifted by integer multiples of \(20\pi/\tau\); assume no overlap.
1. (1 point) Find \(T_s\) and \(P(j\omega)\).
2. (1 point) Recover \(X(j\omega)\).
3. (1 point) Find \(x(t)\) explicitly.
4. (1 point) Express \(g(t)\) as a weighted impulse train; give weights \(m=0,\pm5\).
5. (1 point) Sketch central and nearest groups, explain recovery without aliasing.
solution:
Step 1 — Spectral replica spacing \(\omega_s=20\pi/\tau\) implies \(T_s=2\pi/\omega_s=\tau/10\). Thus
\[P(j\omega)=\frac{20\pi}{\tau}\sum_k\delta(\omega-20\pi k/\tau).\]
Step 2 — With no overlap, central \(G=X/T_s\). Multiply band height 5 by \(T_s=\tau/10\): original band height \(\tau/2\). Hence
\[X(j\omega)=\frac\tau2\left[\operatorname{rect}((\omega-3\pi/\tau)\tau/(2\pi))+\operatorname{rect}((\omega+3\pi/\tau)\tau/(2\pi))\right].\]
Step 3 — Inverse CTFT of shifted rectangles gives a modulated sinc:
\[x(t)=\frac12(e^{j3\pi t/\tau}+e^{-j3\pi t/\tau})\operatorname{sinc}(\pi t/\tau)=\operatorname{sinc}(\pi t/\tau)\cos(3\pi t/\tau).\]
Step 4 —
\[g(t)=\sum_m\operatorname{sinc}(\pi m/10)\cos(3\pi m/10)\delta(t-m\tau/10).\]
Weights: \(w_0=1\), \(w_{\pm5}=\operatorname{sinc}(\pi/2)\cos(3\pi/2)=0\).
Step 5 — Central group has two height-5 bands on stated intervals. Other groups translate boundaries by \(\pm20\pi/\tau\). Highest original nonzero frequency is \(4\pi/\tau\), so \(\omega_s=20\pi/\tau>8\pi/\tau\); neighboring groups cannot overlap. Recover original \(X\) from central group by scaling by \(T_s\).
final_answer: \(T_s=\tau/10\), \(x(t)=\operatorname{sinc}(\pi t/\tau)\cos(3\pi t/\tau)\). Sample weights \(w_0=1,w_{\pm5}=0\), nonoverlapping pairs of rectangular replicas.
variation_strategy: Infer unknown original from sampled frequency domain
generation_rationale: Unlike REF_001, reverse reconstruct sampling interval, original bandpass spectrum and modulated time-domain signal from measured sampled spectrum.

subject: Computer Engineering Mathematics II
learning_objective: Identify convolution operations from partially observed outputs, recover missing samples, and detect an inconsistent output.
question_text:
Three sequences indexed from n=0 to 3 are
\[a[n]=(1,-1,2,0),\quad b[n]=(1,1,-1,0),\quad c[n]=(2,0,-1,1).\]
Four recordings are produced; each valid output uses either full linear or 4-point circular convolution of two DISTINCT sequences from a,b,c. Some measurements are missing (□); one output is inconsistent with all permitted convolutions:
\[Y_1=(2,2,-3,\square,2,-1,0),\]
\[Y_2=(2,-2,3,2,\square,2,0),\]
\[Y_3=(\square,0,0,3),\]
\[Y_4=(1,0,0,2,-2,0,0).\]
1. (2 points) Identify pair/type for Y1, recover missing sample.
2. (2 points) Identify pair/type for Y2, recover missing sample.
3. (2 points) Identify pair/type for Y3, recover missing sample.
4. (2 points) Is Y4 possible? Justify using a mathematical property of convolution. Show calculations; circular convolution length N=4.
solution:
Step 1 — Full linear convolution of two length-4 sequences has length 7; 4-point circular convolution has length 4.
Step 2 — Polynomial representations \(A(z)=1-z+2z^2\), \(B(z)=1+z-z^2\), \(C(z)=2-z^2+z^3\). Their products give
\[B(z)C(z)=2+2z-3z^2+2z^4-z^5,\]
so \(b*c=(2,2,-3,0,2,-1,0)\). Hence \(Y_1=b*c\) and missing value 0.
Likewise
\[A(z)C(z)=2-2z+3z^2+2z^3-3z^4+2z^5,\]
so \(a*c=(2,-2,3,2,-3,2,0)\). Hence \(Y_2=a*c\) and missing value -3.
Step 3 — \(a*b=(1,0,0,3,-2,0,0)\). Folding indices modulo 4 gives \(a*_4b=(1+(-2),0,0,3)=(-1,0,0,3)\). Hence \(Y_3=a*_4b\) and missing value -1.
Step 4 — Convolution preserves the total-sum product: \(\sum_ny[n]=(\sum_nx[n])(\sum_nh[n])\), for linear or circular (over one period). Input sums: \(\sum a=2\), \(\sum b=1\), \(\sum c=2\); distinct-pair sums are 2 or 4. But \(\sum Y_4=1\), so Y4 cannot arise from any allowed pair/type.
final_answer: Y1 = b*c (linear), □=0; Y2=a*c (linear), □=-3; Y3=a*_4b (circular), □=-1; Y4 invalid by sum property (sum=1, allowed sums 2 or 4).

generation_rationale: Partially observed convolution matching with missing samples and a consistency proof, unlike fully observed matching in REF_002.

subject: Computer Engineering Mathematics II
learning_objective: Distinguish full linear versus circular convolution and explain circular folding instead of truncation.
question_text:
Given \(a[n]=(2,-1,1,2)\), \(b[n]=(1,2,-1,1)\), both on \(0\le n\le3\), zero elsewhere. A lab produces
\[R_A=(2,3,-3,7,2,-1,2),\quad R_B=(4,2,\square,7),\quad R_C=(2,3,-3,7).\]
Permitted operations are full linear convolution or 4-point circular convolution of a,b; a recording may be an incorrect or truncated representation.
1. (2 points) Calculate all seven samples of \(y=a*b\).
2. (2 points) Calculate the four samples of \(z=a*_4b\).
3. (2 points) Classify RA,RB,RC and recover missing RB value.
4. (2 points) Determine whether circular convolution is just the first four samples of linear convolution, with mathematical justification.
solution:
Step 1 — Full linear convolution \(y[n]=\sum_k a[k]b[n-k]\), length 7. Direct evaluations:
\[y[0]=2,\ y[1]=4-1=3,\ y[2]=-2-2+1=-3,\]
\[y[3]=2+1+2+2=7,\ y[4]=-1-1+4=2,\ y[5]=1-2=-1,\ y[6]=2.\]
So \(y=(2,3,-3,7,2,-1,2)\).
Step 2 — Circular convolution \(z[n]=\sum_{k=0}^3a[k]b[(n-k)\bmod4]\). Directly,
\[z[0]=2(1)+(-1)(1)+1(-1)+2(2)=4,\]
\[z[1]=2(2)+(-1)(1)+1(1)+2(-1)=2,\]
\[z[2]=2(-1)+(-1)(2)+1(1)+2(1)=-1,\]
\[z[3]=2(1)+(-1)(-1)+1(2)+2(1)=7.\]
Hence \(z=(4,2,-1,7)\).
Step 3 — \(R_A\) is full linear convolution, \(R_B\) is circular convolution with missing -1, and \(R_C\) is a truncated linear output (not a valid full linear or circular result).
Step 4 — In general \(z[n]=\sum_\ell y[n+4\ell]\). For this example, \(z=(y[0]+y[4],y[1]+y[5],y[2]+y[6],y[3])=(4,2,-1,7)\). First four linear samples are \((2,3,-3,7)\). Thus simple truncation is incorrect: circular convolution folds the tail into the beginning.
final_answer: \(a*b=(2,3,-3,7,2,-1,2)\); \(a*_4b=(4,2,-1,7)\). RA linear, RB circular with □=-1, RC truncated/incorrect. Circular convolution uses folding, not truncation.
variation_strategy: Same inputs under two operators with a false truncation claim
generation_rationale: Compared with REF_002, uses the same pair for two operations and requires identifying a truncated-recording misconception.

subject: Computer Engineering Mathematics II
learning_objective: Use impulse support and modular indexing to determine which convolution operation can produce each recording.
question_text:
\[x[n]=\delta[n]+2\delta[n-4],\quad h_1[n]=\delta[n]-\delta[n-3],\quad h_2[n]=\delta[n]+\delta[n-2].\]
Each valid lab recording comes from full linear or 6-point circular convolution of x with h1 or h2:
A: finite output nonzero at (index,value) {(0,1),(3,-1),(4,2),(7,-2)}.
B: 6-periodic, one period (1,-2,0,-1,2,0).
C: 6-periodic, one period (3,0,1,0,2,0).
D: 6-periodic, one period (3,0,1,0,0,2).
Unspecified finite-output samples are zero; periodic outputs repeat indefinitely.
1. (2 points) Identify operation/filter for A.
2. (2 points) Identify B and justify nonzero locations.
3. (2 points) Identify C and explain wrap-around.
4. (2 points) Determine whether D can be produced; justify by convolution support.
solution:
Step 1 — Delta convolution shifts impulses:
\[x*h_1=\delta[n]-\delta[n-3]+2\delta[n-4]-2\delta[n-7].\]
\[x*h_2=\delta[n]+\delta[n-2]+2\delta[n-4]+2\delta[n-6].\]
Step 2 — The support and values of \(x*h_1\) match A exactly, so \(A=x*h_1\) (linear).
Step 3 — Fold \(x*h_1\) modulo 6: indices 0→0,3→3,4→4,7→1. The circular period is \((1,-2,0,-1,2,0)\). So \(B=x*_6h_1\).
Step 4 — Fold \(x*h_2\) modulo 6: indices 0 and 6 collide at index 0, giving 1+2=3; 2 has 1 and 4 has 2. Period \((3,0,1,0,2,0)\). So \(C=x*_6h_2\).
Step 5 — D is nonzero at index 5. Circularly folded support for h1 is {0,1,3,4} and h2 is {0,2,4}; neither permits index 5. Neither full linear convolution is nonzero at n=5 either. Therefore D is impossible.
final_answer: A = x*h1 (linear), B = x*_6 h1 (circular), C = x*_6 h2 (circular), D invalid (index 5 cannot be nonzero).

generation_rationale: Unlike REF_002 graph matching, uses sparse impulse support, modular folding, and impossibility proof by support sets.

subject: Computer Engineering Mathematics II
learning_objective: Understand how cancellation permits distinct input-filter pairs to produce the same linear and circular outputs.
question_text:
Inputs \(r[n]=(1,1,1,1)\), \(s[n]=(1,-1,1,-1)\), and filters \(h_+[n]=(1,1)\), \(h_-[n]=(1,-1)\); all start at n=0 and are zero elsewhere.
Recorded outputs: \(Y_A=(1,0,0,0,-1)\), \(Y_B=(1,2,2,2,1)\), \(Y_C=(1,-2,2,-2,1)\), \(Y_D=(0,0,0,0)\).
Records A–C are linear convolution; D is one period of 4-point circular convolution. More than one pair may be correct.
1. (2 points) Identify ALL input-filter combinations for YA.
2. (2 points) Identify combination for YB.
3. (2 points) Identify combination for YC.
4. (2 points) Identify ALL combinations for YD and explain cancellation.
solution:
Step 1 — Convolution with \(h_+\) implements \(y[n]=x[n]+x[n-1]\), and with \(h_-\) implements \(y[n]=x[n]-x[n-1]\).
The four linear results are:
\[r*h_+=(1,2,2,2,1),\quad r*h_-=(1,0,0,0,-1),\]
\[s*h_+=(1,0,0,0,-1),\quad s*h_-=(1,-2,2,-2,1).\]
Step 2 — Accordingly, \(Y_A=r*h_-\) OR \(s*h_+\), \(Y_B=r*h_+\), \(Y_C=s*h_-\). YA is not uniquely identifiable.
Step 3 — A 4-point circular convolution folds the length-5 linear output's last sample into the first: \(y_4[0]=y[0]+y[4]\), remaining indices 1–3 unchanged. Thus
\[r*_4h_+=(2,2,2,2),\quad r*_4h_-=(0,0,0,0),\]
\[s*_4h_+=(0,0,0,0),\quad s*_4h_-=(2,-2,2,-2).\]
Step 4 — \(Y_D\) can arise from \(r*_4h_-\) OR \(s*_4h_+\). In each, the nonzero linear end values +1 and -1 fold to the same circular index and cancel.
final_answer: YA = r*h- or s*h+; YB = r*h+; YC = s*h-; YD = r*_4 h- or s*_4 h+ (zero from circular cancellation).
variation_strategy: Nonuniqueness and signal cancellation
generation_rationale: Explores nonunique convolution matching and complete enumeration of equivalent input-filter pairs rather than single-pair matching.

subject: Computer Engineering Mathematics II
learning_objective: Evaluate coefficient and convergence claims for a periodic rectangular signal.
question_text:
A continuous-time periodic signal has \(T=6\), defined on \(-3\le t<3\):

subject: Computer Engineering Mathematics II
learning_objective: Derive a closed-form causal inverse filter for a two-echo channel.
question_text:
Acoustic channel
\[h(t)=\delta(t)-\frac34\delta(t-T)+\frac18\delta(t-2T),\quad T>0.\]
Compensation filter \(g(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}g_k\delta(t-kT)\) should exactly recover arbitrary input.

2. (1 point) Derive recurrence for gk, including g0,g1,g2.
3. (2 points) Obtain closed form gk and write complete inverse impulse response.
solution:
Step 1 — Recorded output y=h*x; corrected signal z=g*y=(g*h)*x. Perfect recovery for every x iff \(h*g=\delta\), the identity of convolution.
Step 2 — Match coefficient of \(\delta(t-kT)\): \(g_k-(3/4)g_{k-1}+(1/8)g_{k-2}\), with \(g_{-1}=g_{-2}=0\). Matching δ gives \(g_0=1\) and for k≥1
\[g_k=\frac34g_{k-1}-\frac18g_{k-2}.\]
Thus \(g_1=3/4\) and \(g_2=(3/4)^2-1/8=7/16\).
Step 3 — Formal delay transform \(H(z)=1-(3/4)z+(1/8)z^2=(1-z/2)(1-z/4)\). Invert:
\[G(z)=1/H(z)=\frac2{1-z/2}-\frac1{1-z/4}.\]
For causal geometric powers, \(g_k=2(1/2)^k-(1/4)^k\) for k≥0, so
\[g(t)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}[2(1/2)^k-(1/4)^k]\delta(t-kT).\]
Both terms decay absolutely, so inverse is causal with summable coefficients.

subject: Computer Engineering Mathematics II
learning_objective: Determine whether a causal inverse exists and derive one with a required time advance.
question_text:
Acoustic channel
\[h(t)=\delta(t-T)+\frac13\delta(t-2T),\quad T>0.\]
Compensation filter requires exact zero-delay recovery \(g*h*x=x\) for arbitrary inputs.
1. (2 points) Can a causal inverse achieve this without added delay? Justify.
2. (3 points) Permit one advanced impulse:
\[g(t)=\sum_{n=-1}^{\infty}g_n\delta(t-nT).\]
Derive coefficient recurrence and closed-form g_n.
solution:
Step 1 — Exact recovery requires \(h*g=\delta\). The channel has earliest support at t=T>0; convolving it with a causal g (support t≥0) cannot produce an impulse at t=0. Hence no causal zero-delay inverse.
Step 2 — With \(g(t)=\sum_{n=-1}^{\infty}g_n\delta(t-nT)\), the coefficient of \(\delta(t-mT)\) in h*g is \(g_{m-1}+(1/3)g_{m-2}\), with coefficients below -1 zero.
Step 3 — At m=0, \(g_{-1}=1\). For m≥1, \(g_{m-1}+(1/3)g_{m-2}=0\), or \(g_n=-(1/3)g_{n-1}\) for n≥0. Thus \(g_{-1}=1,g_0=-1/3,g_1=1/9,g_2=-1/27\).
Step 4 — Closed form
\[g_n=(-1/3)^{n+1},\quad n\ge-1,\]
\[g(t)=\sum_{n=-1}^\infty(-1/3)^{n+1}\delta(t-nT).\]
Equivalently \(g(t)=\delta(t+T)-(1/3)\delta(t)+(1/9)\delta(t-T)-\cdots\). Delay-transform verification: \(H(z)=z(1+z/3)\), \(G(z)=z^{-1}/(1+z/3)\), product 1.
final_answer: No causal perfect zero-delay inverse exists. \(g(t)=\sum_{n=-1}^{\infty}(-1/3)^{n+1}\delta(t-nT)\), with a required impulse at t=-T.
variation_strategy: Noncausal advance due to delayed echo
generation_rationale: Adds noncausal invertibility and delay support, distinguishing mathematical inverse from implementable real-time inverse.

subject: Computer Engineering Mathematics II
subtopic: Finite inverse approximation and residual echo
learning_objective: Derive a finite inverse approximation and quantify residual echoes due to truncation.
question_text:
Echo channel
\[h(t)=\delta(t)+\frac23\delta(t-T),\quad T>0.\]
Approximate ideal inverse by \(g_M(t)=\sum_{k=0}^Mg_k\delta(t-kT)\).
1. (1 point) State/justify perfect inverse condition.
2. (1 point) Derive recurrence for ideal gk.
3. (2 points) For M=2, obtain g2(t) and compute overall h*g2.
4. (1 point) Find smallest integer M≥0 for which residual echo coefficient magnitude is strictly below 0.1.
solution:
Step 1 — For arbitrary input exact recovery requires \(h*g=\delta\), since δ is convolution identity.
Step 2 — Match coefficients in \((\delta+(2/3)\delta_T)*\sum_{k\ge0}g_k\delta_{kT}\): \(g_0=1\), \(g_k+(2/3)g_{k-1}=0\) for k≥1. Hence \(g_k=(-2/3)^k\).
Step 3 — For M=2: \(g_0=1,g_1=-2/3,g_2=4/9\), so
\[g_2(t)=\delta(t)-\tfrac23\delta(t-T)+\tfrac49\delta(t-2T).\]
Convolution with h cancels coefficients at delays T and 2T, leaving
\[(h*g_2)(t)=\delta(t)+\frac8{27}\delta(t-3T).\]
Thus for input x, output \(z(t)=x(t)+(8/27)x(t-3T)\).
Step 4 — The finite geometric identity \((1+az)\sum_{k=0}^M(-az)^k=1-(-az)^{M+1}\) yields
\[(h*g_M)(t)=\delta(t)-(-2/3)^{M+1}\delta(t-(M+1)T).\]
Residual magnitude \((2/3)^{M+1}\). Require \((2/3)^{M+1}<0.1\), so \(M+1>\ln(0.1)/\ln(2/3)\approx5.68\). Smallest integer M=5. Check \((2/3)^6=64/729\approx0.0878<0.1\), but \((2/3)^5\approx0.1317\ge0.1\).
